name: Pipe Dream No. 7 (The Long Shift)
description:
No one knows who wrote 'Pipe Dream No. 7.' It exists in dozens of regional variants, each shaped by the specific work environment that adopted it — the maintenance tunnel crews sing it in a slow 6/8 that matches the rhythm of a wrench turning against resistant pipe; the dockworkers' version is faster, syncopated to loading crane cycles; the recycling plant workers in the Shelf's Oku Quarter have a version with an extra verse about the smell of burning insulation that no other variant includes. The earliest documented recording dates to 2188, but workers interviewed in ethnographic surveys consistently describe it as something they learned from someone older, who learned it from someone older still.

Musically, the song is built on a repeating modal phrase of unclear origin — ethnomusicologists have identified structural similarities to Malian griot work traditions, to Norwegian sea shanties, and to a specific rhythmic pattern used in Okinawan agricultural songs, but no single lineage explains it. The lyrics, in all versions, describe the same thing: the psychological landscape of a very long shift, the way time distorts when your body is doing repetitive work, the small negotiations you make with exhaustion, and a final verse about going home that is either deeply hopeful or heartbreaking depending on how it's sung.
creator: traditional (origin unknown)
genre: Contemporary Work Song, Industrial Folk, Oral Tradition
audience: Manual laborers, maintenance crews, dock workers, factory floor workers, recycling and sanitation workers — predominantly Tier 1 and Tier 2; occasionally studied and performed by Tier 3 folk revivalists
cultural_impact: The song functions as social glue in the working layers of GLMZ, a shared vocabulary across wildly different work environments and ethnic backgrounds. Because it has no fixed author and no canonical version, it belongs to everyone who sings it, which is precisely the point. Vantablack Media attempted to register a copyright on one variant in 2211 through a shell imprint, which generated significant public anger and was ultimately unsuccessful due to the documented existence of earlier variants predating the claimed composition date. The attempt is now cited in labor law discussions as an example of cultural enclosure. Ethnomusicology students have documented over forty distinct regional variants; workers generally regard this academic attention with affectionate contempt.
story_hooks: A Vantablack Media IP enforcement agent is tasked with suppressing unauthorized commercial use of the 2211 variant registration — but the more versions they encounter, the more they suspect the song contains something encoded in the melodic variation between versions, something being passed along deliberately.

A Tier 4 executive hears a maintenance crew singing 'Pipe Dream No. 7' in a corridor below their office level and recognizes the tune — their grandmother sang it, and they had no idea it was a work song; the encounter forces them to reckon with a family history they were raised to forget.

Two workers from rival factions — one Shelf, one Circuit, in the middle of a resource dispute — discover they both know the song, different verses, and spend a dangerous night in a flooded maintenance tunnel teaching each other their versions.
